title: a handrail made of sound
hook: your mind already loops a phrase all day; a mantra is choosing which one
tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha, the remover of obstacles. Your line was clear the road, then begin. Did you name what was in the way? And look back: namaste, om, dharma, shanti, pranam, Ganesha. Six words. Day seven.

Nine in the morning, a song from the grocery store slips into someone's head, and it's still looping at lunch. Or it isn't a song. It's a sentence from last night's argument, or a worry about money, going around and around on its own. Nobody chose it. The mind grabbed a phrase and kept playing it. That isn't a personal flaw. Minds do that. The practice of mantra meets that habit with a practical question instead of a fight. If the mind is going to repeat something anyway, what if you picked what it repeats?
screen: `A PHRASE ON A LOOP.` → `NOBODY CHOSE IT.` → `WHAT IF YOU PICKED IT?`

segments.voice: Mantra. The Sanskrit dictionary takes it from man, to think, with tra, an instrument. An instrument of thought. A tool for the mind. And a traditional explanation hears a second meaning: the tra of protection, so a mantra is what protects the mind that dwells on it. You've already met a few. Om, from day two. Om shanti shanti shanti, from day four. Shri ganeshaya namah, from yesterday. There are many more. One is a single verse of the Rig Veda, the Gayatri mantra. In it, the one praying meditates on the bright, worthy light of the god Savitar, the sun as the power that rouses and sets things moving, and asks that he stir and guide our thoughts. A prayer about thinking, said to train the thinking. The Bhagavad Gita gives repetition a place of honor. In the tenth chapter, Krishna lists the forms in which he can be found, and among offerings, he says, he is japa: the quiet repetition of a mantra. Here's how it works in practice. The mind can only hold so much at once. If it's holding the mantra, there's less room for the replay. It's less like a spell and more like a handrail. On a dark staircase, you don't stop to study the dark. You put your hand on the rail and keep going. When the loop comes back, you don't argue with it. You go back to the rail. That's the whole move. Six days ago the strand started with namaste. Now there are seven words on it, and three things you've said along the way, om, the shantis and the line to Ganesha, turn out to have been mantras all along.
screen: `MAN — TO THINK. TRA — A TOOL.` · `OM, SHANTI, THE GAYATRI.` · `AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA.` · `THE LOOP COMES BACK. SO DO YOU.` · then, large: `A HANDRAIL MADE OF SOUND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, with the mantra you already know. Breathe in. On the way out, say om, silently, just in the mind. Again: in, and om. If something else drifts in, a song, a list, a worry, don't push it away. Just put your hand back on the rail. Third breath. In. Om. And notice whether it gave you somewhere to go.
Mantra. An instrument of thought, a tool for the mind, repeated on purpose. Seventh word. A week's worth.
screen: `MANTRA — your 7th word` → the strand, seven lit → `WEEK ONE. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: a handrail made of sound. Today, once, when the replay starts, put your hand on the rail. Om, three times, silently. See what happens. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each one. Tomorrow, the flower, the flame and the bell. Day seven.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOUR GRANDMOTHER WAS ACTUALLY DOING.`

howItsDone: Hindus repeat mantras aloud, in a whisper or silently, sometimes counting them on a string of prayer beads called a mala; this repetition is called japa, and the Gayatri mantra is recited at dawn and dusk by some families.

fork.setup: you're three breaths into saying om silently, and the song from the grocery store comes back. what does the practice ask?
options: argue the song out of your head.
put your hand back on the rail: om.
give up and try again tomorrow.
fork.reveal: you don't fight the loop. you go back to the mantra. the coming back is the practice.

original.note: Sanskrit: man, to think, plus tra, an instrument. an instrument of thought.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant, or a catchy motto.
what it means: a tool for the mind, repeated on purpose, so the mind has something to hold.
what a scholar hears: man + tra, an instrument of thought; a traditional gloss hears trana, protection. Gita 10.25: among offerings, japa.

notes: Gayatri (Rig Veda 3.62.10) paraphrased: meditate on the excellent light of the god Savitr, that he may stir our thoughts. Script says 'Savitri, the divine sun'; Keeper may prefer the Vedic form Savitr/Savitar. Confirm the paraphrase and whether the Keeper wants the Gayatri named on day 7 at all, given that some traditions restrict its recitation.
Gita 10.25 (yajnanam japa-yajno 'smi) paraphrased as 'among offerings, he is japa'; confirm.
Mantra from man + -tra (instrument) follows Monier-Williams; the protection gloss (manana-trana) is attributed to 'a traditional explanation'. Confirm.

Cut from manuscript day 7 under the claims rule: 'about three thousand years ago', 'Man: the same root as the English word' (mind), 'there are thousands', 'most people who've said om namah shivaya ten thousand times couldn't parse it', 'Most people who start something quit before day seven', and 'the mind can't hold two things at once' (softened to 'can only hold so much at once').
Week-end: review lists the week's six words; teach closes on seven.

Audit pass: Savitar is no longer flatly 'the sun' (in the Rig Veda Savitr is the solar god as impeller, distinct from Surya); hook no longer claims what 'this tradition' set out to do; the vague 'the one that holds the others' replaced with which earlier words are mantras.

Editor pass: Gayatri paraphrase corrected from 'the light of Savitri, the divine sun' to 'the god Savitar' (the verse addresses Savitr; Savitri is the verse's own name, not the god's), and it is Savitar who is asked to stir our thoughts, in the teach and the myth reveal; 'a week ago you had none of these words' cut (it told the listener what they knew, and day 1 assumes many already say namaste); 'seven words you can say and mean' (narrator assigning belief) changed to 'seven words, and what's inside each one'.
Editor review 2: closing line said three of the seven strand words were mantras, but 'the line to Ganesha' is not a strand word; now 'three things you've said along the way'.
